metadata.title: Local, World and Screen Space
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: One point, three sets of numbers, and how to switch
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation (canvas item shader reference, shading language, viewport and canvas transforms); Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Local, World and Screen Space. Learn why one point has three sets of numbers, and how a shader switches between them to pin an effect to a sprite, the world or the screen.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. A shader is handed a position, and it is tempting to treat that as a plain fact. It is not. A position is an address in some space, and the same point has a different address in every space.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Six terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture on screen. An origin is where the numbers are zero. A space is a way of measuring positions from one origin. A vertex is a corner point of a shape. And a texture is an image a shader can read by address.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
one dot of the picture on screen
where the numbers are zero; the middle of a centered sprite
a way of measuring positions from one origin
a corner point of a shape
an image a shader can read by address

beats.narration_text: A position is two numbers, and they mean nothing until you say where zero is. From this zero, the dot is five across and four down. Move the zero, and the same dot is one across and three down.

The zero marker then slides to a cell four across and one down; the readout counts to '1 across · 3 down' while the dot never moves.

beats.narration_text: Godot gives you three zeros that matter. The sprite's own center: local space. The world's origin: world space. The window's top-left corner: screen space. One corner of one sprite has an address in each.

shot.visual_intent: One scene on the cream stage: a large outlined rectangle for the world with a zero marker at its top-left labelled 'world space'; inside it a smaller outlined rectangle for the window; inside that a sprite (square outline with the test blob) with a zero marker at its center labelled 'local space'; a third zero marker at the window's top-left labelled 'screen space'. Short definitions appear with each label: 'from the node's own zero', 'from the world's origin' and, for the third, the glossary wording 'pixels of the window, counted from the top left, y growing downward'. A terracotta dot marks the sprite's top-left corner and stays through the act.

beats.narration_text: A shader starts out in local space. The vertex function runs once for each corner, and a built-in called vertex holds that corner's position in pixels. Its zero is the node's own: the center of a sprite, the top-left corner of a color rect.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'From Local to World' (serif 40) top-left. On the left a sprite (square outline, test blob) with a zero marker at its center; its four corners flash in turn with the tags '(-64,-64)', '(64,-64)', '(-64,64)', '(64,64)', a chip 'VERTEX' riding each tag, and a small card 'vertex(): runs once for each vertex; places the corners' with a counter 'run 1, 2, 3, 4' that steps as each corner flashes. On the right a color rect (outlined rectangle) with its zero marker at its top-left corner and the tags '(0, 0)', '(300, 0)', '(0, 200)', '(300, 200)'. A second small card: 'built-in: a value the engine hands to a function, or collects from it'.

beats.narration_text: Why a matrix at all? Adding the node's position handles a plain shift. Add a turn and a change of size, and the corner lands somewhere else entirely. One matrix holds the shift, the turn and the size together.

shot.visual_intent: A sprite outline at the world's zero with its corner dot. Step one: it is shifted to (600, 400) and a grey ghost corner lands at (536, 336), labelled 'add the position'. Step two: the sprite is also turned and doubled in size; the true corner dot lands somewhere else at (553, 225) while the ghost stays at (536, 336), with a short grey arrow between them. A small 4x4 table appears with the card 'matrix: a grid of numbers that moves a point when you multiply by it' and the caption 'one matrix holds shift, turn and size'.

beats.narration_text: That matrix is called model matrix. It stores the node's whole placement: position, turn and size, parents included. Multiply a corner by it, and the corner's world numbers come out.

The sprite travels along an arrow through the table and lands at its place at the right with the tag '(536, 336)'. A small 'parents included' chip appears under the table.

beats.narration_text: Here is that as code. Wrap the corner in a vec four, multiply by the model matrix, and keep the first two numbers. The result is a vec two: the corner's world position.

shot.visual_intent: The line world_position = (MODEL_MATRIX * vec4(VERTEX, 0.0, 1.0)).xy; assembled token by token in monospace. Under it a data strip: the corner '(-64, -64)' becomes '(-64, -64, 0, 1)' as vec4 closes round VERTEX, then '(536, 336, 0, 1)' as MODEL_MATRIX multiplies in, then '(536, 336)' as .xy keeps two. A grey bracket moves under each token as it lands, and a small grey label 'vector: a bundle of two to four numbers' appears under vec4 as the two numbers become four.

beats.narration_text: Why a zero and a one? The matrix keeps the node's shift in its last column. The final one switches that column on, so the corner counts as a place. With a zero instead, the shift is skipped: a direction, not a place.

shot.visual_intent: A 4 by 4 grid of outline cells with the last column outlined and filled with the node's numbers '600, 400, 0, 1' beside the vector '(-64, -64, 0, w)'. With w = 1 a terracotta ring sits on the one and the result reads '(536, 336)' labelled 'a place'. The one then flips to zero: the last column dims and the result falls back to '(-64, -64)' labelled 'a direction'.

lecture.why: The last column and the final one are a picture of a matrix; flipping the one to a zero and watching the answer fall back is the claim as motion.

beats.narration_text: Fragment runs once for each pixel, and it cannot read this matrix. Ask, and the compiler stops you: unknown identifier. Only the vertex function can see model matrix. So how does a pixel learn where it is in the world?

The title says the log was trimmed of its backtrace.

beats.narration_text: With a varying: a value set at each corner, blended across the shape. Vertex stores the world position at the four corners. The graphics card blends them, so every pixel gets its own world position for fragment to read.

shot.visual_intent: A rectangle with four terracotta corner dots; each corner shows its world number ('536, 336', '664, 336', '536, 464', '664, 464'). Inside, a pixel grid of outline cells tints from the corners inward: the red channel as a smooth ramp from the left pair to the right pair, each cell showing a tiny blended value. Card: 'varying: a value set at each corner, blended across the shape for fragment() to read'.
shot.motion_claim: The four corner values flow inward and the cells between them fill with smoothly blended values.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: Four known values becoming a value for every pixel in between is the mechanism; the real render comes in the next beat.

beats.narration_text: Here it is working. The world position becomes the color: red for across, green for down. Slide the sprite, and its colors change, because the sprite is a window onto a color field that stays where it is.

beats.narration_text: Back to the stars. A texture is normally looked up by U V, which is local space squeezed to run from zero to one. Local in pixels or local in U V, the picture belongs to the sprite.

The zero marker slides from the center to the top-left corner while the center's numbers squeeze: '(-64,-64)' becomes '(0, 0)' and '(64, 64)' becomes '(1, 1)'. Card: 'UV: a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'. A small 'stuck to the sprite' chip.

beats.narration_text: World position counts pixels, but a texture wants an address from zero to one. So divide by a tile size you choose. At five hundred twelve, one copy of the picture covers five hundred twelve world pixels, and then the next copy starts.

shot.visual_intent: A horizontal world axis from 0 to about 1500 with tick marks at 512 and 1024. A terracotta dot travels along it; below, a plot of 'address' against world x: a sawtooth that rises from 0 to 1 and wraps back to 0 at every 512, with the dot's current address as a live readout. Label: 'tile size 512'.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A divide and a wrap are a function reshaping a ramp; the dot on the sawtooth is that function in motion.

beats.narration_text: Past one, the address runs off the picture's edge. Mark the texture repeat enable, and the picture tiles forever. Leave it off, and the edge pixels smear outward, like this.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. A position is an address, and each space has its own zero.
